transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45 mins | Attendees: Sabrina (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Ivy (Product), Liam (Bridgewater Head Eng), Priya (Security), Hannah (Product), Raj (SRE)

[00:00] Sabrina: hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Sabrina from Redwood, i'm the account lead for Bridgewater, really appreciate you making time. we have marco and ivy on the call to run through our data handling / retention controls demo, focused on logging redaction, pii detection and the request storage toggles.

[00:18] Liam: thanks, Sabrina. short context — we're a payments processor, we're pci scoped, all customer-facing requests can contain card metadata or pii, so we need clear controls for not retaining sensitive request payloads and to prove that in audits. timeline is tight, want a pilot in q2.

[00:35] Marco: great, totally get it. i'll share my screen — starting with the console first then we'll show API flags and optimize recommendations. quick note: some of my verbalizations may be a bit off in the transcript (auto captions), apologies in advance.

[00:50] Marco: in the console you'll see a Data Controls tab — we have toggle for "store requests" at the project and route level, so you can disable persistent storage globally or for specific endpoints that carry pci/phi. you can also set route-level ttl for request retention, e.g. 7 days, 30 days, or custom.

[01:12] Priya: when you say store requests off at route level, is that full payload never logged anywhere? what about transient logs for debugging?

[01:20] Marco: good question. when you toggle store_requests: false that disables persistent request storage — we still have ephemeral logs in-memory for 60 seconds for request tracing but they are never written to durable storage or included in analytics exports. for debugging you can temporarily enable session-level captures with an expiration and manual purge.

[01:40] Hannah: can you do conditional toggles? e.g., keep storage on for non-sensitive flows but off for anything that matches a payment pattern?

[01:48] Marco: yes — you can attach policies by route or by regex on path or header values. we also support allow/deny lists and attribute-based rules in the UI. so you could have /payments/* default to store_requests: false and /inbox/* remain true.

[02:05] Raj: what about pii redaction — my team wants deterministic redaction for things like card numbers, emails, ssn. are those regex-based or do you have ML-based detectors?

[02:15] Marco: we support both. out-of-the-box we ship regex patterns for common tokens (cards, emails) plus an ML-assisted detector that finds likely pii and suggests redaction rules. you can apply automatic redaction that replaces tokens with placeholders, or you can use hashing/encryption via KMS for reversible tokens.

[02:38] Priya: reversible tokens worry me — auditors ask for key separation and rotation. what's your KMS story?

[02:44] Ivy: we integrate with customer-managed KMS — AWS KMS, Google KMS, or HSMs. keys can be customer-owned and we never store plaintext when configured with customer KMS. we also provide key rotation guidelines and log key usage in audit logs.

[03:02] Liam: good. can you show me how the audit log looks? we need a trail for admin actions and data access for the compliance folder.

[03:10] Marco: sure — switching to the audit section. you can filter by user, action (config change, access, purge), date range and we expose an exportable CSV with actor, timestamp, resource id. note that the audit log itself can be configured to redact sensitive fields on export.

[03:30] Priya: does Redwood support SSO / SAML and role-based access control? we want least privilege for engineers vs security operations.

[03:36] Sabrina: yes — SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning, plus RBAC with fine-grained roles (view-only, admin, retention-manager, etc.). you can tie roles to specific projects or routes.

[03:50] Hannah: how do we prove to auditors that requests with card numbers were never retained? like an immutable proof?

[03:58] Marco: we have an attestation feature — when store_requests is false, the platform marks those requests with a non-reversible indicator and you can export a filtered audit that shows request ids and a retention flag. for added assurance we provide a signed manifest of config changes and key metadata for the audit period.

[04:22] Raj: performance is important — any latency penalty for redaction or route-level checks? our SLAs require sub-100ms p95 for some routes.

[04:30] Marco: the inline regex redaction adds negligible latency (<5ms typical). ML-based detectors run async by default, and we can apply non-blocking redaction or preflight detection. for strict sync redaction we recommend using compiled regex rules at the runtime which are optimized at kernel level. we can run benchmarks with your traffic to validate.

[04:58] Liam: will this work on dedicated or private deployments? we might want private for PCI scoped flows.

[05:06] Marco: absolutely — the same controls are available in hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. for private you get customer-managed control plane and network isolation. we can also provide an on-prem package if required.

[05:18] Priya: about request storage toggles — is that an API flag? can we control it programmatically in CI/CD?

[05:25] Marco: yes, it's exposed via the Redwood API and infra-as-code templates. you can version retention policies and roll them with your release. we also support canary policies for rollout.

[05:38] Hannah: curious about the developer workflow — if i have a dev environment, can i enable full request logging there and disable in prod?

[05:45] Ivy: yes, environments are first-class — dev, staging, prod. retention and redaction settings are environment-scoped and you can use policies to sync or differ across envs.

[05:58] Priya: a corner case — what about third-party integrations that need the full payload? we sometimes share raw events to analytics vendors under contract. can we export raw events for a subset while still meeting PCI requirements?

[06:10] Marco: we support export sinks with filters. you can configure an export that only includes non-sensitive routes or apply field-level redaction before export. for exports that require raw data we recommend using a customer-controlled S3 bucket with envelope encryption via KMS and strict IAM roles.

[06:30] Liam: sounds rigorous. a few objections from finance we expect: cost of retention vs value — how granular can we be on retention policy to save storage costs?

[06:40] Ivy: retention is per-route and per-environment, and we provide cost estimates in the console — you can see projected storage spend based on retention windows and request volume. Optimize will also recommend TTLs and caching to reduce unit costs.

[06:55] Sabrina: quick demo of API for toggling: POST /projects/:id/routes/:route_id with {"store_requests": false, "retention_days": 7} — Marco please show the curl.

[07:05] Marco: yep, copying curl now, executing — returned 200, route updated. on the console the route immediately reflects store_requests: false.

[07:18] Priya: are there logs that show who toggled the flag and when?

[07:22] Marco: yes, that's in the audit log and in the change history for the resource. every API request is audited and correlated to the authenticated user.

[07:35] Hannah: what's the demo POC look like?

[07:38] Sabrina: we proposed a two-week pilot: Redwood sets up a test tenant, Bridgewater provides a sample traffic set and pii patterns, we'll run the retention toggles and run a functional test and perf benchmark. success criteria: 1) retention toggles function as expected, 2) no retained sensitive payloads for flagged routes, 3) performance impact within agreed budget.

[07:58] Liam: ok. small thing — sometimes auto redaction misses edge cases, how do we iterate?

[08:04] Marco: we provide a redaction rule editor and a preview tool where you can run sample payloads and see matched tokens; you can add custom regex or ML-suggested patterns. we also store false-positive/false-negative examples so the ML detector improves over the POC.

[08:22] Priya: any certifications we can share? SOC2 type II, iso?

[08:27] Sabrina: we'll share SOC2 type II report and our security whitepaper. for private deployments we can accommodate additional third-party audits as part of enterprise agreements.

[08:40] Raj: one more technical: do you keep kv cache or any parts of the model state that could leak information?

[08:46] Marco: good callout — Redwood's serving runtime keeps ephemeral kv cache for active sessions but it's cleared on session end. for private/dedicated customers we can configure cache encryption and disable cross-request caching for sensitive endpoints.

[09:02] Hannah: ok thanks. can we get a copy of the recording and the slides?

[09:06] Sabrina: yes, i'll send the recording and the security deck after the call.

[09:12] Marco: final note — i'll set up the test tenant and send instructions for providing sample traffic.

[09:18] Sabrina: recap — Sabrina to share SOC2/encryption docs, Marco to set up tenant and retention toggles, Bridgewater (Priya & Liam) to send sample PII patterns and traffic. schedule POC check-in 2026-04-27. anyone else?

[09:36] Liam: that's everything, thanks all.

[09:40] Sabrina: thanks, talk soon. bye.

End of transcript. Some speaker labels may have been auto-attributed (e.g., "Marco" might show as Speaker 2). There are brief disfluencies and auto-caption artifacts.
